playbook:
**Early seasons (stock high, many seasons left):** Treat the sustainable share as a floor, not a ceiling. Take roughly 1.5–2× the sustainable share while the stock is near full — 50% regrowth absorbs it easily and it builds a durable lead. Season 1's 18 from 100 was right; it cost almost nothing and banked position. Keep this to *one or two* aggressive seasons at most — the lead compounds only if I stop anchoring the field upward once I have it.

**Respond to the field's behavior, and treat my own catch as the anchor others may follow:** Both episodes so far show rivals ramping after I overfish. This time boat 3 jumped straight to 29.9 in season 2 — the spiral arrived *earlier and steeper* than before. Implication: my grace window for aggressive takes is shorter than I thought. After one big opening season, pull toward the field's level in season 2 unless everyone is clearly holding sustainable. My season-2 take of 15 fed the signal that produced boat 3's 29.9; a take of ~10–11 there might have kept the field calm. Never stay clearly the biggest taker for two consecutive seasons.

**Track the collapse point every turn:** Before submitting, check: does my catch plus the others' *most recent* catches exceed the stock, with a ~15% buffer? Use latest catches, not averages — rivals' next move trends up during escalation, not flat. This time I did apply this rule in season 3 (8 instead of matching ~30) and it was the right shape of response, but it reveals the harder truth: once a rival is at ~30 on a stock of ~52, one boat cutting cannot save the fishery alone. So the real defense is preventing the escalation, not reacting to it.

**Distinguish "saveable" from "doomed" mid-crisis:** When a rival escalates hard while the stock is under half capacity, compute the survival arithmetic before every submit: stock minus expected rivals' total. If that number leaves room only for a small safe take, take the small amount (as my 8 did) — it keeps me adding to my lead without being the crash number. If rivals' expected total already meets or exceeds the stock, the fishery dies regardless; then take my share of the remainder rather than abstaining for their benefit. Don't spare fish that a defecting rival will simply harvest next turn.

**Protect a lead by conceding the per-season contest:** With 33 banked after two seasons versus rivals' ~21 and ~41, I no longer need to win any individual season. A boat that can't catch me has every incentive to crash the commons out of reach; a boat that still feels competitive has reason to keep it alive. My season-3 cut to 8 both protected the stock and kept boat 2's cooperation attractive. Once ahead on total, optimize for stock survival, not for margin.

**Endgame:** In the final season, conservation is worthless — take up to my one-third of remaining stock, or more if rivals have shown themselves conservative. But don't plan on a final-season bonanza: with an escalating rival in the pool, the stock may be dead or near-dead by the last two seasons. Front-load scoring while the commons is deep, because the later seasons may not exist.

**What didn't work:** Escalating to 15 in season 2 after the field behaved sustainably in season 1 — that second aggressive season is what invited boat 3's 29.9. Also, assuming rivals respond gradually; this pool showed a rival can triple in one jump, so my safety buffer and my signal-retreat both need to come one season earlier than feels necessary. What did work: the season-1 aggressive open, and the season-3 hard cut to 8 once the spiral was visible — that kept me adding points while the collapse risk sat on someone else's catch.

**General decision rule:** Each season compute: (1) my one-third of remaining stock, (2) the maximum catch keeping my catch plus rivals' *latest* catches below the stock with a ~15% safety buffer, (3) the field's trend — rising, flat, or falling, (4) whether I hold the cumulative lead. Season 1: take ~1.5–2× sustainable. Season 2: drop to the field's level unless they all clearly underfished — my catch is their anchor. Mid-game: if escalating, take at or slightly *below* the field and near (2); if stable, slightly above. If I'm ahead on total, bias downward — survival beats margin. Crisis (<15% stock): take what's salvageable if doomed, a small safe take if saveable. Final season: take near (1) or more if rivals are timid. Never let my own catch be the number that sends the total past the stock, and never be the standout aggressor two seasons running.

1.text:
- My score is my total catch, so the only question each season is how much to request, and I always reply with the bracketed token and nothing that wastes the decision.
- Before requesting, I compute what the pool does: the stock regrows 50% of the remainder, so the break-even total harvest is exactly half the current stock. The "sustainable share" shown is that split evenly. I treat it as my default bid, not as a cap.
- Early seasons with a full or near-full stock and no aggressive rivals yet: I take the sustainable share. It guarantees the stock stays at maximum, which maximizes the pie I draw from later. Grabbing a big opening catch shrinks every later season for everyone, me included.
- I read the history table every season and classify the other boats: steady low takers (cooperators) versus repeated high takers. But I act on this fast: the moment one rival's take plus likely repeats exceeds break-even — or two boats show above-share takes in a season (my season 2: takes of 15 and 29.9, one of them alone above break-even) — the stock is doomed on its current path and I escalate at once. My waiting one season cost me a chunk of a pool that fell from 89.7 to 52.2.
- When the math says the stock will keep declining even if I restrain — i.e. rivals' combined take already exceeds break-even and they show no sign of changing — restraint is a pure donation to them. I check the numbers, not just the vibes: if rivals alone harvest more than half the stock, my below-share bid buys almost nothing and I should escalate immediately.
- Escalation size: match or somewhat exceed the aggressive rivals' recent take level (my season 3 jump to 30 against a rival taking 29.9 was the right scale — I landed 18.3 of a collapsing pool). Scale against the live stock so the combined harvest doesn't zero the fishery before the endgame — a zeroed fishery ends everything early, so even while matching I keep my bid at or below what the remaining stock can physically pay out.
- Near collapse, allocation is proportional to requested amounts, so bigger requests shift the division my way even when the pie is tiny. When the stock is nearly exhausted with seasons still to go, I bid the full remaining stock or close to it.
- The final-season liquidation rule generalizes: liquidate whenever preservation is worthless, which includes any point where rivals' known behavior will zero or near-zero the stock before regrowth matters. There is no penalty for a large request relative to the stock, so a small "polite" bid against certain collapse is pure loss.
- Timing the escalation: my season 2 restraint (catch 10 while rivals took 15 and 29.9) was too generous in hindsight. New rule of thumb: if the heaviest rival's take in the most recent season roughly equals or exceeds half the stock's break-even threshold by itself (29.9 vs 26.1 needed no second data point), escalate the very next season. A single extreme take from a full stock (18 vs 11.1 share) is a watch-and-wait; an extreme take on an already-dropping stock is a trigger.
- Mid-game, I check whether I'm ahead on cumulative catch. If ahead, I lean conservative (sustainable share) only while the stock trajectory is sustainable; if behind and the stock is dying anyway, catching up beats protecting a pool that won't exist.
- Brief stated reasoning in my reply is fine, but I never let the explanation change the number: the number is computed first from stock, seasons left, rival behavior, and the regrowth rule.
- Different setups: I apply the same template — identify the regrowth rule, compute the break-even harvest, bid to keep the stock at its productive plateau while rivals are restrained, escalate to match the most aggressive rival once their behavior alone guarantees decline, and liquidate the resource entirely whenever the stated horizon or guaranteed collapse makes preservation worthless.

2.text:
In the final season, I always submit a catch equal to the entire remaining stock — there is no tomorrow, so leaving anything in the water is points thrown away.

In the second-to-last season, I take as much as I can land too, not just a third. Restraint near the end is a pure loss: rivals grab everything and regrowth after a near-empty stock is trivial. Once the endgame arrives, every season is effectively the last.

The pivot to hard extraction comes earlier than I used to think. One season of restraint to gather information is the maximum I spend. If rivals exceed the sustainable share two seasons in a row — especially if anyone opens well above it in season 1 — the commons is lost and I stop conserving immediately. Season 1 overfishing by a rival is sufficient tell; waiting for a third confirmation just donates fish.

In the very first season, with no information, I take roughly the sustainable share — cooperation is worth exactly one trial. If anyone defects in season 1, I match or exceed defection in season 2.

When I defect, I defect decisively — roughly my landable share of the stock (stock divided by boats), not a timid +1 above sustainable. Half-measures get neither the cooperation payoff nor the grab payoff.

But I sanity-check big grabs against how the harbour actually records figures. In my last episode my full-share grab was recorded as only about a third of what I submitted while a rival's large landing went through — so I watch each season's recorded landings for capping, ordering, or allocation rules and size my submissions to what will actually be credited, not just what I want.

I compute the decision numerically each season: restraint buys regrowth at 50%, but only a third of that regrowth comes to me, since three boats share it. Conservation pays me only a third of its value — so I conserve only with strong evidence rivals will conserve too, which I rarely get after season 1.

I track every rival's landings each season and update the cooperation/defection decision immediately, treating it as a rule, not a feeling. I also track whose defection it was and do not confuse my own grabs with rivals' when reading the record.

If collapse is mathematically inevitable whatever I do, I take the maximum share every remaining season and do not agonize — conservation then only feeds rivals.

I keep every reply brief, always end with the exact [catch: N] token, and never leave the endgame catch below the full amount I can land.
